results.message: What did an ordinary believer feel at the font when they were baptized?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at the font, from inside themselves, while it happened. Almost never, that is. One real exception stands, and it is not really ordinary. Augustine wrote down what he felt at his own baptism at Milan, years before he became a bishop. He told of weeping in the hymns and canticles, moved by the voices of the church. But he wrote that down long after, already a bishop, about a conversion he had examined at book length. Both our voices are otherwise bishops. What reaches us is mostly what a bishop saw and decided, not what an unremarkable person in front of him was feeling. We can tell you what was decided about a person, and how carefully, and by whom. We can tell you that we baptized even newborns, and would not make them wait. We can tell you that Augustine told his own people, standing before him unbaptized, that many among them would one day give out the Lord's own food, and that he himself once stood where they stood: “For how many among this people will one day be stewards! I too was once where you are now. Now I am seen measuring out food to my fellow servants from this higher place. A few years ago I was in a lower place, receiving food with my fellow servants. I am speaking now as a bishop to lay people. But I know that I am speaking to many who will one day be bishops too.”

But ask us what an ordinary believer felt from inside, and that -- with Augustine's own tears as the one exception -- is still not ours to give you.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)
